interactions: Tamsulosin: no clinically significant interaction expected.
Acetaminophen (paracetamol) up to 650 mg three times daily as needed: no pharmacokinetic interaction and no change needed at this dose; consider it when interpreting a transaminase rise.

Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for the first 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x ULN. action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, most marked in the right tibialis anterior, with chronic neurogenic change in the right first dorsal interosseous and tibialis anterior, normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block, and normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral corticospinal tract T2/FLAIR hyperintensity (supportive only); no mass, hemorrhage, infarct, demyelinating lesion or calvarial marrow lesion.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No cord compression, cord signal abnormality, epidural mass or vertebral marrow lesion from the cervical to the lumbosacral spine; mild L4-L5 and L5-S1 degenerative changes without root compression.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up. Here the lumbosacral spine is included because the presentation is a right foot drop in a man with prostate cancer.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 740 U/L (4.3x ULN); normal blood count, renal and liver function, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: SNIP 68 cmH2O and NIF -52 cmH2O reduced (NIF meets an AAN 2009 marker), FVC 80% predicted at the lower limit of normal.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansion and no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction with tamsulosin; as-needed acetaminophen and light alcohol use need no change; transaminases before the first dose and on the monitoring schedule, stopping riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x ULN.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. Tamsulosin does not interact with it, and as-needed acetaminophen at his dose needs no change but is considered when interpreting a transaminase rise.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
Do not refer for lumbar spine surgery on the basis of the L4-L5 and L5-S1 degenerative changes: they do not explain the upper motor neuron signs or denervation beyond the lumbosacral roots.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive right lower limb weakness with foot drop, spreading to the right hand, with upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, brisk biceps and knee reflexes, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs, spastic gait) and lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in bulbar and thoracic muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now and discuss NIV: NIF -52 cmH2O meets an AAN 2009 marker of respiratory insufficiency (SNIP 68 cmH2O is also reduced); assess orthopnoea and overnight oximetry or capnography to time NIV, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk jaw jerk, brisk biceps and knee reflexes, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs and a spastic gait with lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions, with active denervation also in bulbar and thoracic muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy or SBMA.
CK 740 U/L (4.3x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

SNIP 68 cmH2O and NIF -52 cmH2O are reduced and FVC 80% predicted is at the lower limit of normal; NIF -52 cmH2O meets an AAN 2009 marker. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

Lumbar degenerative changes are common at this age and cannot explain upper motor neuron signs or denervation in bulbar, cervical and thoracic muscles. Lumbosacral paraspinal denervation localises the lesion proximal to the intervertebral foramina, so it occurs in both L5 radiculopathy and anterior horn cell disease; the spread beyond the lumbosacral segments decides.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Low-risk prostate cancer on active surveillance with a stable PSA and no metastasis on oncology imaging or spine MRI is very unlikely to cause a compressive or paraneoplastic syndrome; no paraneoplastic panel was done, and the combined upper and lower motor neuron signs with denervation in four regions fit ALS.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a metastatic or paraneoplastic explanation for the new neurological syndrome

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The degenerative changes cause no root compression, and an L5 radiculopathy cannot explain bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs, tongue fasciculations or denervation in bulbar, cervical and thoracic muscles.
red_herrings.data_point: Right foot drop with mild L4-L5 and L5-S1 degenerative changes
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent to attribute the foot drop to an L5 radiculopathy

mri.impression: 1. Bilateral symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of the corticospinal tracts from the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the cerebral peduncles. No mass, hemorrhage, infarct or demyelinating lesion. No calvarial or skull-base marrow lesion.

findings.finding: Right FDI: fibrillations +2, large MUPs. Right APB: fibrillations +1. Bilateral paraspinals C5-C7: fibrillations +1.

Right tibialis anterior: fibrillations +3, positive sharp waves +3, markedly reduced recruitment. Left tibialis anterior: fibrillations +1. Right gastrocnemius: fasciculations. Lumbosacral paraspinals L3-L5: fibrillations +1.
Superficial peroneal, sural and median sensory responses: normal amplitudes and conduction velocities.

Right peroneal motor: CMAP amplitude 1.4 mV (markedly reduced; reference >2 mV), normal conduction velocity 44 m/s. No conduction block. Right median motor: CMAP amplitude reduced, normal distal latency and conduction velocity, no conduction block. Right ulnar and right tibial motor: normal CMAP amplitudes, distal latencies and conduction velocities, no conduction block or temporal dispersion.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Active denervation (fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves) in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, most marked in the right tibialis anterior, including cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral (L3-L5) paraspinal muscles; chronic neurogenic change with large motor unit potentials in the right first dorsal interosseous and markedly reduced recruitment in the right tibialis anterior; fasciculations in the tongue and right gastrocnemius. 2. Reduced right peroneal and right median CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block in any nerve tested. 3. Normal sensory conduction studies. Findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells, consistent with a motor neuron disease.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Prostate cancer on active surveillance and a right foot drop with lumbar degenerative changes raise metastatic, paraneoplastic and radicular mimics that the work-up excludes; otherwise classic ALS with 4 required studies.
metadata.notes: ALS presenting with right foot drop in a 72-year-old man with low-risk prostate cancer on active surveillance; spinal metastasis and L5 radiculopathy are excluded, and lumbosacral paraspinal denervation does not by itself separate radiculopathy from anterior horn cell disease.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W is a 72-year-old retired insurance adjuster with a history of low-grade prostate cancer on active surveillance who presents with a 12-month history of progressive right leg weakness and foot drop. He first noticed difficulty lifting his right foot approximately 12 months ago, initially thinking he had sprained his ankle. However, no ankle injury was documented and the weakness has steadily worsened without any mechanism of injury. Over the following months, he developed bilateral arm fasciculations that his wife noticed during dinner, and he reports progressive weakness of his right hand making it difficult to open jars and turn door handles. He has no back pain, no bowel or bladder dysfunction, and no sensory loss in any distribution. His prostate cancer has been under active surveillance with stable PSA at 3.2 ng/mL — he has had no bone scan or CT suggesting metastatic disease. His oncologist performed imaging 8 months ago that showed no evidence of metastatic disease. He denies any new urinary symptoms. The neurological symptoms have progressed in a relentless ascending pattern and he has had no plateaus or episodes of recovery.
